title: Children of Adam
intro: Saadi of Shiraz finished the *Golestan* ('The Rose Garden'), a book of short stories in prose mixed with verse, in 1258. In the tenth story of the first chapter, *On the conduct of kings*, he is praying at the tomb of John the Baptist in the Great Mosque of Damascus when a king known for his injustice asks for his prayers. Saadi tells him to be merciful to the weak, and ends with these six lines. They are probably the best-known Persian poem in the world: Iranian children learn them at school, people quote them after every earthquake and flood, and they are woven into a carpet at the United Nations in New York.

lines.fa: بنی‌آدم اعضای یکدیگرند / که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند
lines.r: bani-ādam a'zā-ye yekdigar-and / ke dar āfarinesh ze yek gowhar-and
lines.en: The children of Adam are limbs of one another, / for in creation they are made of one essence.
lines.note: Many people quote the first half as «بنی‌آدم اعضای یک پیکرند» *bani-ādam a'zā-ye yek peykar-and* – 'are limbs of one body'. The standard editions of the *Golestan* have یکدیگرند 'of one another'.
words: the children of Adam, humankind (Arabic بنی 'sons of')
from, of – the poetic short form of از

lines.fa: چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار / دگر عضوها را نماند قرار
lines.r: cho 'ozvi be dard āvarad ruzgār / degar 'ozv-hā rā namānad gharār
lines.en: When the world brings pain to one limb, / the other limbs can find no rest.
words: when; like – poetic form of چون
to bring to pain, to hurt

lines.fa: تو کز محنت دیگران بی‌غمی / نشاید که نامت نهند آدمی
lines.r: to kaz mehnat-e digarān bi-ghami / nashāyad ke nām-at nahand ādami
lines.en: You who feel no grief at the suffering of others / do not deserve to be called human.
lines.lit: you who from the suffering of others are without-sorrow, it is not fitting that they put your name 'human'
words: who … from – که + از run together
without sorrow, carefree; بی‌غمی 'you are carefree'
it is not fitting (from the old verb شایستن)
to give a name, to call

commentary:
**The image.** Saadi takes a picture everyone understands – the body – and makes it a rule of conduct. When one finger is burnt, the whole body feels it and cannot sleep; in the same way, one person's pain should trouble everyone. The image echoes a well-known saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, that believers are like one body, and Saadi widens it from believers to all the children of Adam.

**The rhythm.** The lines are in *motaqāreb*, the metre of Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh* and of Saadi's own *Bustan*: four beats to a half-line, *da-DUM-DUM da-DUM-DUM da-DUM-DUM da-DUM*. Read the first half-line slowly: *ba-ni ā-dam a'-zā-ye yek-di-ga-rand*. Each couplet has its own rhyme – [[یکدیگرند|yekdigar-and]] / [[گوهرند|gowhar-and]], [[روزگار|ruzgār]] / [[قرار|gharār]], [[بی‌غمی|bi-ghami]] / [[آدمی|ādami]].

**The grammar.** Classical poetry uses short forms you will now recognise everywhere: [[ز|ze]] for [[از|az]], [[چو|cho]] for [[چون|chon]], [[دگر|degar]] for [[دیگر|digar]], [[کز|kaz]] for [[که از|ke az]]. The verbs [[آورد|āvarad]] and [[نماند|namānad]] have no [[می|mi]]: in the classical language this simple present states a general truth – 'whenever the world hurts one limb, the others do not stay at rest'. In modern prose you would say [[وقتی روزگار عضوی را به درد می‌آورد، عضوهای دیگر آرام نمی‌مانند|vaghti ruzgār 'ozvi rā be dard mi-āvarad, 'ozv-hā-ye digar ārām nemi-mānand]].

**Using it.** Iranians quote the first line, or just the words *bani-ādam*, to say that a disaster far away concerns us all. The last couplet is the sharp one: it is quoted at people who shrug at others' suffering.
